# Reviving a Series III Land Rover After Ten Months of Storage

Restarting a vehicle that has sat for ten months requires shifting your mindset from routine maintenance to systematic preservation and verification. Your 1973 Land Rover SWB Series III with the Holden 202ci inline-six presents specific challenges due to its age, dual-fuel conversion history, and prolonged inactivity. While topping up fluids and greasing fittings are standard procedures, they address only half of the equation. The real work lies in mitigating internal corrosion and ensuring the fuel system is ready for a cold start.

Your battery voltage reading of 12.54V after ten months with a trickle charger is encouraging, indicating it hasn't sulfated or deeply discharged yet. However, rely on this only as a preliminary check. Before attempting to crank the engine, measure the specific gravity if you have access to hydrometers, or better yet, perform a load test once the engine starts. A 12V system under no-load can sit high, but under load, voltage should remain above 9.6V during cranking and settle around 13.5–14.0V when running on LPG. If it drops below that threshold immediately after starting, you have a charging system issue before you even get moving.

Regarding the cylinder lubrication strategy you considered: removing spark plugs to inject clean engine oil is plausible but carries risks if not executed precisely. The goal is to coat the cylinder walls and piston rings without flooding the combustion chamber or damaging the ignition coil mounting hardware. For an inline-six like yours, this can be tedious due to limited access compared to a V-engine. A more controlled approach involves using a dedicated canister of compressed air with an oil additive designed for winterizing or engine preservation. Spray small bursts directly into each cylinder while the plugs are out, then reinstall the plugs immediately to prevent contamination from external debris entering the intake manifold. This coats the internals without the mess and potential misfire risks associated with liquid pooling near the coil pack.

Fuel system integrity is likely your highest priority given the dual-fuel setup. Even if you intend to run exclusively on LPG, the petrol tank acts as a reservoir where moisture accumulates over time, leading to rust in the sump or sediment buildup. Drain any remaining fuel from both tanks and lines completely. While leaving gasoline in the carburetor float bowl might seem convenient, that fluid is now stale and contaminated with water. Run the engine on LPG for several minutes until you are certain the petrol tank is empty; this clears the transition circuitry and ensures the gas regulator sees only clean fuel. If your LPG mixer valve has been idle, check for seized diaphragms or clogged jets before engaging it fully.

Do not overlook the cooling system. Static conditions allow water to settle at the lowest point of the radiator or heater matrix. Inspect the coolant level and look for signs of localized rust or sludge that may have settled over winter. If the vehicle has been exposed to road salt (common even in milder climates), a flush might be necessary before the next startup. Finally, verify the condition of the brake lines and master cylinder reservoir, as rubber hoses can dry rot internally over ten months regardless of external appearance.

Once you initiate the start sequence, listen closely. A Series III with a Holden engine should fire up relatively quickly if the cylinders were properly lubricated and the battery is healthy. If it cranks without firing, check for spark at all six plugs simultaneously; one bad plug in an older distributor setup can sometimes mislead diagnostics into thinking there's no ignition entirely. If the engine turns over but runs poorly on LPG immediately after startup, let it warm up briefly before engaging the throttle to allow the lubrication to distribute through the bearings and clear any residual condensation from the intake tract.
